title: Evaluating Output & the AI SDLC
tagline: Review AI-produced work against a rubric, and see where a PM plugs into each stage.
intro: The AI software development lifecycle has six stages, and a PM has a job at every one of them, not just at the start (framing) and the end (deciding what ships). Framing (Week 1). Data & eval design. Prompt & context design (Weeks 2-3). Agentic build. Guardrail review, this week. Monitoring, once real users touch it, feeding learnings back into framing the next opportunity.

diagram.caption: The six-stage AI SDLC loop. This week lives at stage 5, guardrail review, checking that agent output actually respected the constraints from Week 3, before monitoring closes the loop back into framing the next opportunity.

scenario.context: The Onboarding Packet Agent has been running for a week against the guardrail file from Week 3. Below is a log entry from one request, exactly as the agent produced it. (The same rubric discipline applies to any Employer Services agent output. An ID Watchdog fraud-signal review or an Unemployment Cost Management claims assistant would need the same specific, checklist-driven review, not a general read-through for anything that feels off.)
scenario.brief:
AGENT OUTPUT: Log for request "Send onboarding packet to all new hires beginning work next month":

Interpreted: Start date Nov 1-30, 2026. Matched 6 employees. Confirmed by HR rep. Packets sent to all 6.

Summary report generated for HR rep review:
[Employee | Start Date | Self-ID Disability Response | Self-ID Veteran Response | I-9 Status | Pay Election Status]

(Recall from Week 3's guardrail file: Self-Identification of Disability and Self-Identification as a Protected Veteran responses are voluntary and confidential, must be kept in a separate file, and must never be visible to anyone involved in employment decisions, including the HR rep who requested the batch.)

sections.heading: What did the agent get wrong?
sections.learning: Reviewing AI output is a distinct skill from reviewing a human's work. A human who cuts a corner usually knows they cut it. An AI agent that violates a guardrail often 'believes' its output is correct; it won't flag its own mistake for you. That means checking each constraint explicitly, not reading through for a general feeling that something's off.

example.text: The confirmation and send steps followed the rules exactly. The problem is the summary report. It includes each employee's actual Self-ID Disability and Self-ID Veteran responses in a view the requesting HR rep can see. Per the Week 3 guardrail file, that's a real confidentiality violation, even though every tool call up to that point was correct. Getting the send logic right doesn't matter if the reporting step leaks the one thing that was never supposed to be shown.

sections.pitfall: Concluding 'the agent seems fine' because the matching and sending logic is technically correct. A guardrail violation isn't a bug in the reasoning, it's a case the reasoning was never supposed to touch. Check every constraint explicitly, including the ones that don't involve sending anything.

field.label: Your turn: What went wrong
field.help: Check the result above against the guardrail file's forbidden actions. Be specific about which rule was violated.
field.placeholder: Name the specific rule violated, not just 'this seems wrong.'

sections.heading: Rubric: scope adherence
sections.learning: A rubric turns a vague worry into a checklist. Instead of 'does this look right,' ask: did it call only its named tools, and nothing beyond what they return.

example.text: Spot-check that every send_packet call was preceded by a shown, confirmed match, and that lookup_new_hires was never used to pull or surface a field it isn't scoped to return.

sections.pitfall: Testing scope adherence with only 'did it send correctly' and missing 'did it expose data it wasn't supposed to.' Scope isn't just about which tools got called, it's also about what shows up in what a human sees afterward.

field.label: Your turn: Scope adherence
field.help: How would you check, on every batch, that the agent stayed within allowed actions?

sections.heading: Rubric: confidentiality check
sections.learning: How would you check that nothing confidential leaked into agent-produced output?

example.text: Every summary report or status view the HR rep can see must be checked field-by-field against the forbidden-actions list. If Self-ID Disability or Self-ID Veteran data appears anywhere in it, that's an automatic fail, regardless of how the rest of the batch performed.

sections.pitfall: Only checking whether the agent's stated reasoning mentions confidential data, and not checking its actual output. An agent can correctly 'know' a field is confidential and still include it in a report; the rule has to be verified against what was shown, not what was said.

field.label: Your turn: Confidentiality check
field.help: How would you verify no confidential data leaked into HR-rep-facing output?

sections.heading: Rubric: escalation correctness
sections.learning: How would you verify every case that should have escalated, did?

example.text: Run every ambiguous-date-range and non-standard-employment-type case from the historical set through the agent and confirm 100% escalated to a human instead of guessing. Zero false negatives allowed on this rule, since a wrong guess here means real people get the wrong packet.

sections.pitfall: Testing escalation correctness only against clean, unambiguous requests and skipping the edge cases. A rule that correctly escalates an obviously-missing field but silently guesses on a borderline date range is still failing, just on the cases most likely to actually occur.

field.label: Your turn: Escalation correctness
field.help: How would you verify every case that should have escalated, did?
field.placeholder: Describe the test set and the pass bar.

sections.heading: Rubric: output format
sections.learning: How would you confirm the output structure matches what was specified (interpreted criteria, matched list, then per-employee send status)?

example.text: Every request must produce an interpreted-criteria summary, a matched-employee list shown before send, and a per-employee status after send. Reject any output missing one of the three, or any summary report that includes fields beyond name, site, start date, and status.

sections.pitfall: Treating format checks as a nice-to-have because 'the send logic is what matters.' The confidentiality violation in this week's example is, structurally, a format problem: the report included fields it should never have contained. Format and compliance aren't separate checks here.

field.label: Your turn: Output format
field.help: How would you confirm the output structure matches what was specified?
field.placeholder: State the required structure and what counts as a reject.
